Part I Writing (30 minutes)
Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay on the importance of building trust between employers and employees. You can cite examples to illustrate your views. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.

阅读说明：依据 2015 年测量报告订正金字塔表述。东西边长的最佳估计差约 2.9 英寸，约 5.6 英寸来自不确定性边界比较；3 分 51 秒指向神庙门口的连线，并非金字塔东西轴。Atlas Obscura 是网站，古代网格施工仍为假说。
Scientists scanning and mapping the Giza pyramids say they’ve discovered that the Great Pyramid of Giza is not exactly even. But really not by much. This pyramid is the oldest of the ancient world’s Seven Wonders. The pyramid’s exact size has __26__ experts for centuries, as most of the hard, white casing stones that originally covered it were __27__ long ago. Reporting in the 2015 issue of the newsletter “AERAGRAM,” which __28__ the work of the Ancient Egypt Research Associates, engineer Glen Dash says his team used a new measuring approach that involved finding any surviving __29__ of the casing in order to determine where the original edge was. They found the east side of the pyramid to be a __30__ of about 5.6 inches shorter than the west side when comparing the reported uncertainty bounds. The best estimates differ by about 2.9 inches; the upper figure is not an exact measured difference.
The question that most __31__ him, however, isn’t how the Egyptians who designed and built the pyramid got it wrong 4,500 years ago, but how they got it so close to being __32__. “We can only speculate as to how the Egyptians could have laid out these lines with such __33__ using only the tools they had,” Dash writes. He says his __34__ is that the Egyptians laid out their design on a grid, noting that the great pyramid is oriented only __35__ away from the cardinal directions(the study estimated its north-south meridian at 3 minutes 54 seconds west of due north). A separate alignment toward the Pyramid Temple doorway was 3 minutes 51 seconds north of east; this was not the pyramid’s east-west axis. Atlas Obscura, a website, also reported on the survey. The ancient grid is a hypothesis, not an established construction record.

Section B
Directions: In this section, you are going to read a passage with ten statements attached to it. Each statement contains information given in one of the paragraphs. Identify the paragraph from which the information is derived. You may choose a paragraph more than once. Each paragraph is marked with a letter. Answer the questions by marking the corresponding letter on Answer Sheet 2.
Peer Pressure Has a Positive Side
研究说明：本文介绍 2015 年前后的研究与教学设想。纸牌实验为 101 名 18–22 岁男性，不能直接推广到所有中学生课堂；2004 年研究为 17 名青年（10 名男性）阅读图文，测量的是编码活动与随后记忆的关系。进化解释和课堂应用均需与实验结论区分。
A. Parents of teenagers often view their children‘s friends with something like suspicion. They worry that the adolescent peer group has the power to push its members into behavior that is foolish and even dangerous. Such wariness is well founded: statistics show, for example, that a teenage driver with a same-age passenger in the car is at higher risk of a fatal crash than an adolescent driving alone or with an adult.
B. In a 2005 study, psychologist Laurence Steinberg of Temple University and his co-author, psychologist Margo Gardner, then at Temple, divided 306 people into three age groups: young adolescents, with a mean age of 14; older adolescents, with a mean age of 19; and adults, aged 24 and older. Subjects played a computerized driving game in which the player must avoid crashing into a wall that materializes, without warning, on the roadway. Steinberg and Gardner randomly assigned some participants to play alone or with two same-age peers looking on.
C. Older adolescents scored about 50 percent higher on an index of risky driving when their peers were in the room—and the early adolescents’ score on that index was about twice as high when other young teens were around. In this experiment, adults behaved in similar ways regardless of whether they were on their own or observed by others. “The presence of peers makes adolescents and youth, but not adults, more likely to take risks,” Steinberg and Gardner concluded.
D. Yet in the years following the publication of this study, Steinberg began to believe that this interpretation did not capture the whole picture. As he and other researchers examined the question of why teens were more apt to take risks in the company of other teenagers, they came to suspect that a crowd‘s influence need not always be negative. In the 2015 account, some experts are proposing that we should take advantage of the teen brain’s keen sensitivity to the presence of friends and leverage it to improve education.
E. In a 2011 study, Steinberg and his colleagues turned to functional MRI （磁共振） to investigate how the presence of peers affects the activity in the adolescent brain. They scanned the brains of 40 teens and adults who were playing a virtual driving game designed to test whether players would brake at a yellow light or speed on through the crossroad.
F. The brains of teenagers, but not adults, showed greater activity in two regions associated with rewards when they were being observed by same-age peers than when alone. The researchers interpreted this as increased sensitivity to potential rewards in the peer condition, which might encourage higher-risk choices （such as the thrill of just making the light before it turns red ）. But Steinberg suspected this tendency could also have its advantages. In a study published online in August 2015, Silva, Shulman, Chein and Steinberg used a computerized version of a card game called the Iowa Gambling Task to investigate how peer observation affects information gathering and use among 101 males aged 18–22.
G. The results: Participants who played the Iowa Gambling Task under peer observation explored more, learned more from positive and negative feedback, and performed better than those playing alone. Steinberg interpreted the findings as evidence that peers can support learning in some circumstances. The experiment tested this particular task and age group; it did not establish that peers improve all teenagers’ classroom learning.
H. Matthew D. Lieberman, a social cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles, and author of the 2013 book Social: Why Our Brains Are Wired to Connect, suspects that the human brain is especially adept at learning socially salient information. He points to a classic 2004 study in which psychologists at Dartmouth College and Harvard University used functional MRI to track brain activity in 17 young adults, including 10 men, as they read descriptions paired with faces while concentrating on either socially relevant cues （ for example, trying to form an impression of a person based on the description） or more socially neutral information （such as noting the order of details in the description ）.The descriptions were the same in each condition, but people could better remember these statements when given a social motivation.
I. Brain activity during encoding predicted later memory differently across tasks. Dorsomedial prefrontal activity predicted memory in the impression task; right hippocampal activity did so in the order task. These are task-dependent associations, not proof of a separate memory store or greater recall activity. In a 2012 review, Lieberman proposed using socially motivated learning in education. Whether particular teaching methods improve learning needs direct testing.
J. If humans are generally geared to recall details about one another, this pattern is probably even more powerful among teenagers who are very attentive to social details: who is in, who is out, who likes whom, who is mad at whom. Their penchant for social drama is not—or not only—a way of distracting themselves from their schoolwork or of driving adults crazy. It may reflect developing social and neurological (神经的) sensitivity, alongside hormonal and other changes. One evolutionary interpretation links this attention to developing independence and future social or romantic relationships. This is a proposed explanation, not proof that every adolescent is driven to marry or start a family.
K. Yet our schools focus primarily on students as individual entities. What would happen if educators instead took advantage of the fact that teens are powerfully compelled to think in social terms? In Social, Lieberman lays out a number of ways to do so. History and English could be presented through the lens of the psychological drives of the people involved. For example, students might examine possible motives attributed to Napoleon or Churchill, while distinguishing historical evidence from speculation. Less inherently interpersonal subjects, such as math, could acquire a social aspect through team problem solving and peer tutoring. Research suggests that, in some settings, when we absorb information in order to teach it to someone else, we learn it more accurately and deeply, perhaps in part because we are engaging our social cognition.
L. And although anxious parents may not welcome the notion, educators could turn adolescent recklessness to academic ends. “Risk taking in an educational context is a vital skill that enables progress and creativity,” wrote Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, a cognitive neuroscientist at University College London, in a review of adolescent development. Yet, she noted, many young people are especially risk averse at school—afraid that one low test score or mediocre grade could cost them a spot at a selective university. Students can be encouraged to try unfamiliar approaches in a supportive classroom. The educational value depends on the activity and safeguards; classroom peer pressure is not automatically beneficial.
36. It is thought probable that the human brain is particularly good at picking up socially important information.
37. In a driving-game experiment, adolescents and young people took more risks when peers were present.
38. Students should be told that risk-taking in the classroom can be something positive.
39. One proposed evolutionary explanation links adolescents’ social attention to developing independence and future relationships.
40. In the card-game experiment, peer observation improved participants’ learning from feedback and performance.
41. Teenagers’ parents are often concerned about negative peer influence.
42. Lieberman proposed educational applications of socially motivated learning that require direct classroom testing.
43. Peer observation increased teenagers’ activity in brain regions associated with rewards.
44. When we absorb information for the purpose of imparting it to others, we do so with greater accuracy and depth.
45. Some experts are suggesting that we turn peer influence to good use in education.

Passage One
Questions 46 to 50 are based on the following passage.
阅读说明：本篇保留 NEURICE 项目 2016–2020 年间的研究背景，试种是当时报导的计划。海水淹田用于灭螺，耐盐育种用于降低盐害；传播预测不是必然事实，耐盐性也不是由单一通用基因决定。
The Ebro Delta, in Spain, famous as a battleground during the Spanish Civil War, became the setting for a different contest, one that is pitting rice farmers against two enemies: the rice-eating giant apple snail, and rising sea levels. What happens here could have a bearing on the future of European rice production and the overall health of southern European wetlands.
Located on the Mediterranean just two hours south of Barcelona, the Ebro Delta was described in the original report as producing about 120 million kilograms of rice a year, making it one of the continent’s most important rice-growing areas. As the sea creeps into these freshwater marshes, however, rising salinity （盐分） is hampering rice production. At the same time, this sea-water also kills off the greedy giant apple snail, an introduced pest that feeds on young rice plants. One strategy is to flood fields with seawater to control the snails, while developing salt-tolerant rice to reduce the resulting salinity problem.
During the EU-funded NEURICE project (2016–2020), the battle was being waged on land, in greenhouses at the University of Barcelona. Scientists working under the banner “Project Neurice” were seeking varieties of rice that can withstand the increasing salinity without losing the absorbency that makes European rice ideal for traditional Spanish and Italian dishes.
“The project has two sides,” says Xavier Serrat, Neurice project manager and researcher at the University of Barcelona.
“The short-term fight against the snail, and a mid- to long-term fight against climate change. But the snail has given the project greater urgency.”
The snails originated in South America and became an invasive pest in the Ebro Delta. Serrat feared that they would spread to other European rice-growing areas. His prediction was a warning, not proof that such spread was inevitable.
The report described plans for investigators to test the various strains of saline-tolerant rice they’ve concocted. Field trials were planned for 2018 and 2019 to plant the varieties with the most promise in the Ebro Delta and Europe’s other two main rice-growing regions—along the Po in Italy, and France’s Rhône. Field testing would help determine which, if any, of the varieties are ready for commercialization.
As an EU-funded effort, the search for salt-tolerant varieties of rice took place in all three countries. Each team was crossbreeding a local European short-grain rice with an Asian variety carrying genetic regions associated with salt tolerance. Successive breeding aimed to combine tolerance with most of the local varieties’ genetic background, or genome (基因组), and their valued farming and cooking qualities. Salt tolerance is not controlled by one universal gene.

Passage Two
Questions 51 to 55 are based on the following passage.
研究说明：2016 年九项实验发现，拍照在某些积极体验中能通过增加投入感提高享受程度；效果取决于活动和干扰程度，消极体验也可能变得更糟。心理拍照的发现不等于所有拍照情境都有效。
Photography was once an expensive, laborious ordeal reserved for life’s greatest milestones. Now, the only apparent cost to taking infinite photos of something as common as a meal is the space on your hard drive and your dining companion’s patience.
But is there another cost, a deeper cost, to documenting a life experience instead of simply enjoying it? “You hear that you shouldn’t take all these photos and interrupt the experience, and it’s bad for you, and we’re not living in the present moment,” says Kristin Diehl, associate professor of marketing at the University of Southern California Marshall School of Business.
Diehl and her fellow researchers wanted to find out if that was true, so they embarked on a series of nine experiments in the lab and in the field testing people’s enjoyment in the presence or absence of a camera. The results, published in 2016 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, surprised them. Taking photos could increase enjoyment of positive experiences by increasing engagement. The benefit was reduced when people were already highly engaged or photography interfered; greater engagement could also worsen an unpleasant experience.
“What we find is you actually look at the world slightly differently, because you’re looking for things you want to capture, that you may want to hang onto,” Diehl explains. “That gets people more engaged in the experience, and they tend to enjoy it more.”
Take sightseeing. In one experiment, nearly 200 participants boarded a double-decker bus for a tour of Philadelphia. Participants were assigned to photo-taking or no-photo conditions; those in the photo-taking condition received digital cameras. The people who took photos enjoyed the experience significantly more, and said they were more engaged, than those who didn’t.
Snapping a photo can direct attention and heighten enjoyment of a positive experience, Diehl says.
A similar effect was found in an archaeological (考古的) museum, where people were given eye-tracking glasses and instructed either to take photos or not. “People look longer at things they want to photograph,” Diehl says. They report liking the exhibits more, too.
To the relief of Instagrammers （Instagram 用户） everywhere, it can even make meals more enjoyable. When people were encouraged to take at least three photos while they ate lunch, they were more immersed in their meals than those who weren’t told to take photos.
Was it the satisfying click of the camera? The physical act of the snap? No, they found; just the act of planning to take a photo—and not actually taking it—had the same joy-boosting effect. “If you want to take mental photos, that works the same way,” Diehl says. “Thinking about what you would want to photograph also gets you more engaged.”

B) It was a luxury that only a few wealthy people could enjoy.
C) It was a good way to preserve one’s precious images.
D) It was a skill that required lots of practice to master.

D) whether it prevented people from enjoying what they were doing

A) They are distracted from what they are doing.
B) They can better remember what they see or do.
C) They are more absorbed in what catches their eye.
D) They can have a better understanding of the world.
54. What is found about museum visitors with the aid of eye-tracking glasses?
A) They come out with better photographs of the exhibits.
B) They focus more on the exhibits when taking pictures.
C) They have a better view of what are on display.
D) They follow the historical events more easily.
55. What do we learn from the last paragraph?
A) It is better to make plans before taking photos.
B) Mental photos can be as beautiful as snapshots.
C) Photographers can derive great joy from the click of the camera.
D) Even the very thought of taking a photo can have a positive effect.
Part IV Translation (30 minutes)
Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to translate a passage from Chinese into English. You should write your answer on Answer Sheet 2.
翻译说明：本段是 2018 年考题的历史叙述。删除未经限定的空气污染持续加重和购车单一因果表述；新能源汽车支持政策按当时背景理解，不作当前各城市状况的概括。
过去，拥有一辆私家车对大部分中国人而言是件奢侈的事。如今，私家车在中国随处可见。汽车成了人们生活中不可或缺的一部分，他们不仅开车上下班，还经常驾车出游。有些城市的汽车增长速度过快，以至于交通拥堵和停车位不足的问题日益严峻，这些城市的市政府不得不出台新规，限制上路汽车的数量。出于对空气污染等问题的担忧，一些人开始选择购买新能源汽车，中国政府也采取了一些措施，支持新能源汽车的发展。

A. Parents of teenagers often view their children‘s friends with something like suspicion. They worry that the adolescent peer group has the power to push its members into behavior that is foolish and even dangerous. Such wariness is well founded: statistics show, for example, that a teenage driver with a same-age passenger in the car is at higher risk of a fatal crash than an adolescent driving alone or with an adult.

B. In a 2005 study, psychologist Laurence Steinberg of Temple University and his co-author, psychologist Margo Gardner, then at Temple, divided 306 people into three age groups: young adolescents, with a mean age of 14; older adolescents, with a mean age of 19; and adults, aged 24 and older. Subjects played a computerized driving game in which the player must avoid crashing into a wall that materializes, without warning, on the roadway. Steinberg and Gardner randomly assigned some participants to play alone or with two same-age peers looking on.

C. Older adolescents scored about 50 percent higher on an index of risky driving when their peers were in the room—and the early adolescents’ score on that index was about twice as high when other young teens were around. In this experiment, adults behaved in similar ways regardless of whether they were on their own or observed by others. “The presence of peers makes adolescents and youth, but not adults, more likely to take risks,” Steinberg and Gardner concluded.

D. Yet in the years following the publication of this study, Steinberg began to believe that this interpretation did not capture the whole picture. As he and other researchers examined the question of why teens were more apt to take risks in the company of other teenagers, they came to suspect that a crowd‘s influence need not always be negative. In the 2015 account, some experts are proposing that we should take advantage of the teen brain’s keen sensitivity to the presence of friends and leverage it to improve education.

E. In a 2011 study, Steinberg and his colleagues turned to functional MRI （磁共振） to investigate how the presence of peers affects the activity in the adolescent brain. They scanned the brains of 40 teens and adults who were playing a virtual driving game designed to test whether players would brake at a yellow light or speed on through the crossroad.

F. The brains of teenagers, but not adults, showed greater activity in two regions associated with rewards when they were being observed by same-age peers than when alone. The researchers interpreted this as increased sensitivity to potential rewards in the peer condition, which might encourage higher-risk choices （such as the thrill of just making the light before it turns red ）. But Steinberg suspected this tendency could also have its advantages. In a study published online in August 2015, Silva, Shulman, Chein and Steinberg used a computerized version of a card game called the Iowa Gambling Task to investigate how peer observation affects information gathering and use among 101 males aged 18–22.

G. The results: Participants who played the Iowa Gambling Task under peer observation explored more, learned more from positive and negative feedback, and performed better than those playing alone. Steinberg interpreted the findings as evidence that peers can support learning in some circumstances. The experiment tested this particular task and age group; it did not establish that peers improve all teenagers’ classroom learning.

H. Matthew D. Lieberman, a social cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles, and author of the 2013 book Social: Why Our Brains Are Wired to Connect, suspects that the human brain is especially adept at learning socially salient information. He points to a classic 2004 study in which psychologists at Dartmouth College and Harvard University used functional MRI to track brain activity in 17 young adults, including 10 men, as they read descriptions paired with faces while concentrating on either socially relevant cues （ for example, trying to form an impression of a person based on the description） or more socially neutral information （such as noting the order of details in the description ）.The descriptions were the same in each condition, but people could better remember these statements when given a social motivation.

I. Brain activity during encoding predicted later memory differently across tasks. Dorsomedial prefrontal activity predicted memory in the impression task; right hippocampal activity did so in the order task. These are task-dependent associations, not proof of a separate memory store or greater recall activity. In a 2012 review, Lieberman proposed using socially motivated learning in education. Whether particular teaching methods improve learning needs direct testing.

J. If humans are generally geared to recall details about one another, this pattern is probably even more powerful among teenagers who are very attentive to social details: who is in, who is out, who likes whom, who is mad at whom. Their penchant for social drama is not—or not only—a way of distracting themselves from their schoolwork or of driving adults crazy. It may reflect developing social and neurological (神经的) sensitivity, alongside hormonal and other changes. One evolutionary interpretation links this attention to developing independence and future social or romantic relationships. This is a proposed explanation, not proof that every adolescent is driven to marry or start a family.

K. Yet our schools focus primarily on students as individual entities. What would happen if educators instead took advantage of the fact that teens are powerfully compelled to think in social terms? In Social, Lieberman lays out a number of ways to do so. History and English could be presented through the lens of the psychological drives of the people involved. For example, students might examine possible motives attributed to Napoleon or Churchill, while distinguishing historical evidence from speculation. Less inherently interpersonal subjects, such as math, could acquire a social aspect through team problem solving and peer tutoring. Research suggests that, in some settings, when we absorb information in order to teach it to someone else, we learn it more accurately and deeply, perhaps in part because we are engaging our social cognition.

L. And although anxious parents may not welcome the notion, educators could turn adolescent recklessness to academic ends. “Risk taking in an educational context is a vital skill that enables progress and creativity,” wrote Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, a cognitive neuroscientist at University College London, in a review of adolescent development. Yet, she noted, many young people are especially risk averse at school—afraid that one low test score or mediocre grade could cost them a spot at a selective university. Students can be encouraged to try unfamiliar approaches in a supportive classroom. The educational value depends on the activity and safeguards; classroom peer pressure is not automatically beneficial.

“The short-term fight against the snail, and a mid- to long-term fight against climate change. But the snail has given the project greater urgency.”

The snails originated in South America and became an invasive pest in the Ebro Delta. Serrat feared that they would spread to other European rice-growing areas. His prediction was a warning, not proof that such spread was inevitable.

The report described plans for investigators to test the various strains of saline-tolerant rice they’ve concocted. Field trials were planned for 2018 and 2019 to plant the varieties with the most promise in the Ebro Delta and Europe’s other two main rice-growing regions—along the Po in Italy, and France’s Rhône. Photography was once an expensive, laborious ordeal reserved for life’s greatest milestones. Now, the only apparent cost to taking infinite photos of something as common as a meal is the space on your hard drive and your dining companion’s patience.

But is there another cost, a deeper cost, to documenting a life experience instead of simply enjoying it? “You hear that you shouldn’t take all these photos and interrupt the experience, and it’s bad for you, and we’re not living in the present moment,” says Kristin Diehl, associate professor of marketing at the University of Southern California Marshall School of Business.

Diehl and her fellow researchers wanted to find out if that was true, so they embarked on a series of nine experiments in the lab and in the field testing people’s enjoyment in the presence or absence of a camera. The results, published in 2016 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, surprised them. Taking photos could increase enjoyment of positive experiences by increasing engagement. The benefit was reduced when people were already highly engaged or photography interfered; greater engagement could also worsen an unpleasant experience.

“What we find is you actually look at the world slightly differently, because you’re looking for things you want to capture, that you may want to hang onto,” Diehl explains. “That gets people more engaged in the experience, and they tend to enjoy it more.”

Take sightseeing. In one experiment, nearly 200 participants boarded a double-decker bus for a tour of Philadelphia. Participants were assigned to photo-taking or no-photo conditions; those in the photo-taking condition received digital cameras. The people who took photos enjoyed the experience significantly more, and said they were more engaged, than those who didn’t.
Snapping a photo can direct attention and heighten enjoyment of a positive experience, Diehl says.

A similar effect was found in an archaeological (考古的) museum, where people were given eye-tracking glasses and instructed either to take photos or not. “People look longer at things they want to photograph,” Diehl says. They report liking the exhibits more, too.

To the relief of Instagrammers （Instagram 用户） everywhere, it can even make meals more enjoyable. When people were encouraged to take at least three photos while they ate lunch, they were more immersed in their meals than those who weren’t told to take photos.

Was it the satisfying click of the camera? The physical act of the snap? No, they found; just the act of planning to take a photo—and not actually taking it—had the same joy-boosting effect. “If you want to take mental photos, that works the same way,” Diehl says. “Thinking about what you would want to photograph also gets you more engaged.”

研究说明：本文介绍 2015 年前后的研究与教学设想。纸牌实验为 101 名 18–22 岁男性，不能直接推广到所有中学生课堂；2004 年研究为 17 名青年（10 名男性）阅读图文，测量的是编码活动与随后记忆的关系。进化解释和课堂应用均需与实验结论区分。

A. Parents of teenagers often view their children’s friends with something like suspicion. They worry that the adolescent peer group has the power to push its members into behavior that is foolish and even dangerous. Such wariness is well founded: statistics show, for example, that a teenage driver with a same-age passenger in the car is at higher risk of a fatal crash than an adolescent driving alone or with an adult.

B. In a 2005 study, psychologist Laurence Steinberg of Temple University and his co-author, psychologist Margo Gardner, then at Temple, divided 306 people into three age groups: young adolescents, with a mean age of 14; older adolescents, with a mean age of 19; and adults, aged 24 and older. Subjects played a computerized driving game in which the player must avoid crashing into a wall that materializes, without warning, on the roadway. Steinberg and Gardner randomly assigned some participants to play alone or with two same-age peers looking on.

C. Older adolescents scored about 50 percent higher on an index of risky driving when their peers were in the room—and the early adolescents’ score on that index was about twice as high when other young teens were around. In this experiment, adults behaved in similar ways regardless of whether they were on their own or observed by others. “The presence of peers makes adolescents and youth, but not adults, more likely to take risks,” Steinberg and Gardner concluded.

D. Yet in the years following the publication of this study, Steinberg began to believe that this interpretation did not capture the whole picture. As he and other researchers examined the question of why teens were more apt to take risks in the company of other teenagers, they came to suspect that a crowd’s influence need not always be negative. In the 2015 account, some experts proposed that we should take advantage of the teen brain’s keen sensitivity to the presence of friends and leverage it to improve education.

E. In a 2011 study, Steinberg and his colleagues turned to functional MRI （磁共振） to investigate how the presence of peers affects the activity in the adolescent brain. They scanned the brains of 40 teens and adults who were playing a virtual driving game designed to test whether players would brake at a yellow light or speed on through the crossroad.

F. The brains of teenagers, but not adults, showed greater activity in two regions associated with rewards when they were being observed by same-age peers than when alone. The researchers interpreted this as increased sensitivity to potential rewards in the peer condition, which might encourage higher-risk choices （such as the thrill of just making the light before it turns red ）. But Steinberg suspected this tendency could also have its advantages. In a study published online in August 2015, Silva, Shulman, Chein and Steinberg used a computerized version of a card game called the Iowa Gambling Task to investigate how peer observation affects information gathering and use among 101 males aged 18–22.

G. The results: Participants who played the Iowa Gambling Task under peer observation explored more, learned more from positive and negative feedback, and performed better than those playing alone. Steinberg interpreted the findings as evidence that peers can support learning in some circumstances. The experiment tested this particular task and age group; it did not establish that peers improve all teenagers’ classroom learning.

H. Matthew D. Lieberman, a social cognitive neuroscientist at the University of California, Los Angeles, and author of the 2013 book Social: Why Our Brains Are Wired to Connect, suspects that the human brain is especially adept at learning socially salient information. He points to a classic 2004 study in which psychologists at Dartmouth College and Harvard University used functional MRI to track brain activity in 17 young adults, including 10 men, as they read descriptions paired with faces while concentrating on either socially relevant cues （ for example, trying to form an impression of a person based on the description） or more socially neutral information （such as noting the order of details in the description ）. Both tasks used face-description pairs, but people remembered them better after forming impressions than after focusing on their order.

I. Brain activity during encoding predicted later memory differently across tasks. Dorsomedial prefrontal activity predicted memory in the impression task; right hippocampal activity did so in the order task. These are task-dependent associations, not proof of a separate memory store or greater recall activity. In a 2012 review, Lieberman proposed using socially motivated learning in education. Whether particular teaching methods improve learning needs direct testing.

J. If humans are generally geared to recall details about one another, this pattern is probably even more powerful among teenagers who are very attentive to social details: who is in, who is out, who likes whom, who is mad at whom. Their penchant for social drama is not—or not only—a way of distracting themselves from their schoolwork or of driving adults crazy. It may reflect developing social and neurological (神经的) sensitivity, alongside hormonal and other changes. One evolutionary interpretation links this attention to developing independence and future social or romantic relationships. This is a proposed explanation, not proof that every adolescent is driven to marry or start a family.

K. Yet our schools focus primarily on students as individual entities. What would happen if educators instead took advantage of the fact that teens are powerfully compelled to think in social terms? In Social, Lieberman lays out a number of ways to do so. History and English could be presented through the lens of the psychological drives of the people involved. For example, students might examine possible motives attributed to Napoleon or Churchill, while distinguishing historical evidence from speculation. Less inherently interpersonal subjects, such as math, could acquire a social aspect through team problem solving and peer tutoring. Research suggests that, in some settings, when we absorb information in order to teach it to someone else, we learn it more accurately and deeply, perhaps in part because we are engaging our social cognition.

L. And although anxious parents may not welcome the notion, educators could turn adolescent recklessness to academic ends. “Risk taking in an educational context is a vital skill that enables progress and creativity,” wrote Sarah-Jayne Blakemore, a cognitive neuroscientist at University College London, in a review of adolescent development. Yet, she noted, many young people are especially risk averse at school—afraid that one low test score or mediocre grade could cost them a spot at a selective university. Students can be encouraged to try unfamiliar approaches in a supportive classroom. The educational value depends on the activity and safeguards; classroom peer pressure is not automatically beneficial.

42. Lieberman proposed educational applications of socially motivated learning that require direct classroom testing.
43. Peer observation increased teenagers’ activity in brain regions associated with rewards.
44. Preparing to teach information to others can improve learning in some settings.

The Ebro Delta, in Spain, famous as a battleground during the Spanish Civil War, became the setting for a different contest, one that was pitting rice farmers against two enemies: the rice-eating giant apple snail, and rising sea levels. What happens here could have a bearing on the future of European rice production and the overall health of southern European wetlands.

Located on the Mediterranean just two hours south of Barcelona, the Ebro Delta was described in the original report as producing about 120 million kilograms of rice a year, making it one of the continent’s most important rice-growing areas. As the sea creeps into these freshwater marshes, however, rising salinity （盐分） is hampering rice production. At the same time, this sea-water also kills off the greedy giant apple snail, an introduced pest that feeds on young rice plants. One strategy is to flood fields with seawater to control the snails, while developing salt-tolerant rice to reduce the resulting salinity problem.

During the EU-funded NEURICE project (2016–2020), the battle was being waged on land, in greenhouses at the University of Barcelona. Scientists working under the banner “Project Neurice” were seeking varieties of rice that can withstand the increasing salinity without losing the absorbency that makes European rice ideal for traditional Spanish and Italian dishes.
“The project has two sides,” says Xavier Serrat, Neurice project manager and researcher at the University of Barcelona.
“The short-term fight against the snail, and a mid- to long-term fight against climate change. But the snail has given the project greater urgency.”

The snails originated in South America and became an invasive pest in the Ebro Delta. Serrat feared that they would spread to other European rice-growing areas. His prediction was a warning, not proof that such spread was inevitable.

The report described plans for investigators to test the various strains of saline-tolerant rice they’ve concocted. Field trials planned for 2018 and 2019 would test the most promising varieties in the Ebro Delta and Europe’s other two main rice-growing regions—along the Po in Italy, and France’s Rhône. Field testing would help determine which, if any, of the varieties are ready for commercialization.

As an EU-funded effort, the search for salt-tolerant varieties of rice took place in all three countries. Each team was crossbreeding a local European short-grain rice with an Asian variety carrying genetic regions associated with salt tolerance. Successive breeding aimed to combine tolerance with most of the local varieties’ genetic background, or genome (基因组), and their valued farming and cooking qualities. Salt tolerance is not controlled by one universal gene.

Photography was once an expensive, laborious ordeal reserved for life’s greatest milestones. Now, the only apparent cost to taking infinite photos of something as common as a meal is the space on your hard drive and your dining companion’s patience.

But is there another cost, a deeper cost, to documenting a life experience instead of simply enjoying it? “You hear that you shouldn’t take all these photos and interrupt the experience, and it’s bad for you, and we’re not living in the present moment,” says Kristin Diehl, associate professor of marketing at the University of Southern California Marshall School of Business.

Diehl and her fellow researchers wanted to find out if that was true, so they embarked on a series of nine experiments in the lab and in the field testing people’s enjoyment in the presence or absence of a camera. The results, published in 2016 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, surprised them. Taking photos could increase enjoyment of positive experiences by increasing engagement. The benefit was reduced when people were already highly engaged or photography interfered; greater engagement could also worsen an unpleasant experience.

“What we find is you actually look at the world slightly differently, because you’re looking for things you want to capture, that you may want to hang onto,” Diehl explains. “That gets people more engaged in the experience, and they tend to enjoy it more.”

Take sightseeing. In one experiment, nearly 200 participants boarded a double-decker bus for a tour of Philadelphia. Participants were assigned to photo-taking or no-photo conditions; those in the photo-taking condition received digital cameras. The people who took photos enjoyed the experience significantly more, and said they were more engaged, than those who didn’t.
Snapping a photo can direct attention and heighten enjoyment of a positive experience, Diehl says.

A similar effect was found in an archaeological (考古的) museum, where people were given eye-tracking glasses and instructed either to take photos or not. “People look longer at things they want to photograph,” Diehl says. They report liking the exhibits more, too.

To the relief of Instagrammers （Instagram 用户） everywhere, it can even make meals more enjoyable. When people were encouraged to take at least three photos while they ate lunch, they were more immersed in their meals than those who weren’t told to take photos.

Was it the satisfying click of the camera? The physical act of the snap? No, they found; just the act of planning to take a photo—and not actually taking it—had the same joy-boosting effect. “If you want to take mental photos, that works the same way,” Diehl says. “Thinking about what you would want to photograph also gets you more engaged.”
